business-foundations-1/beat-00.text: Fresh lemonade, made with lemons, sugar and a bit of love! One pound a cup.

business-foundations-1/beat-01.text: Everyone looked so thirsty, so I’ve been giving it away. Look at our queue!

business-foundations-1/beat-02.text: Good on you. I’ll buy more lemons out of my own pocket, I suppose.

business-foundations-1/beat-03.text: A long queue, and an empty tin. A business makes something people want and sells it for more than it cost to make.

business-foundations-1/beat-04.text: Oh! So I take the pound, and the lemons get paid for out of it?

business-foundations-1/beat-06.text: Profit isn’t greed. It’s proof that people valued the lemonade more than it cost to make.

business-foundations-1/beat-07.text: Now we’re both squeezing lemons, and nobody’s serving. Was that my job, or yours?

business-foundations-1/beat-08.text: And that’s the other half of it, called leadership. Someone has to make sure every job has one owner.

business-foundations-1/beat-10.text: Right, I’ll squeeze, you serve, and the pound goes in the tin. Beauty.

business-foundations-2/beat-00.text: Fresh lavender macarons, all in pastel pink! The builders next door are going to love them.

business-foundations-2/beat-01.text: Lovely and dainty. Got anything a person could eat at seven in the morning?

business-foundations-2/beat-02.text: The baker made what she likes, for a customer she imagined. A business starts with the customer at the counter.

business-foundations-2/beat-03.text: Your customer is the person whose problem you solve. His problem is a cold morning, and a long shift ahead.

business-foundations-2/beat-05.text: Sausage rolls, coming right up! Although I’m sure everyone secretly wants a macaron.

business-foundations-2/beat-06.text: That’s a guess, and a guess can be checked. Watch what sells, and ask the people buying it.

business-foundations-2/beat-07.text: Since nobody asked, a bigger cup of tea would be nice. Not that anyone ever asks.

business-foundations-2/beat-09.text: One sausage roll, and one very large tea. Oh, and I’ve written it all down!

business-foundations-3/beat-00.text: Fifty pence a candle! I’d hate for anyone to go without.

business-foundations-3/beat-01.text: Fifty pence? I’d happily pay five pounds for a candle that smells like Christmas!

business-foundations-3/beat-02.text: Every candle costs him wax, a wick, a jar and an hour of work. A price has to cover all of that.

business-foundations-3/beat-03.text: The wax and the jar alone cost two pounds. At fifty pence, every candle he sells makes him poorer.

business-foundations-3/beat-05.text: Oh dear. I’d only ever thought about the people buying them.

business-foundations-3/beat-06.text: Think about them too. Value is what a candle is worth to the customer, and she just told you.

business-foundations-3/beat-07.text: Oh, and six pounds if it comes with a ribbon!

business-foundations-3/beat-08.text: So the price sits between the two: above what it costs to make, and no higher than people will pay.

business-foundations-3/beat-10.text: Four pounds, then. And the ribbon’s on the house, for my first customer.

business-foundations-4/beat-00.text: Three hundred pounds today. As I suspected, I’m a business genius.

business-foundations-4/beat-01.text: Brilliant day! Here are the receipts for the bread, the fuel and the pitch.

business-foundations-4/beat-02.text: The three hundred pounds is your revenue: all the money that came in. It isn’t what you keep.

business-foundations-4/beat-03.text: Costs are what you paid to make those sales. The bread, the fuel and the pitch came to two hundred and twenty pounds.

business-foundations-4/beat-05.text: Fine. So how much of my genius do I get to keep?

business-foundations-4/beat-06.text: Take the costs away from the revenue: three hundred, less two hundred and twenty, leaves eighty pounds. That’s your profit.

business-foundations-4/beat-07.text: Eighty pounds. Still a genius, just a slightly smaller one.

business-foundations-4/beat-08.text: The bakery across the road sells bread for less. If we buy it there, we’ll keep more.

business-foundations-5/beat-00.text: Twelve flights booked this month. That’s three thousand pounds of profit, and I’m a genius of the skies.

business-foundations-5/beat-01.text: Morning! Here’s your gas for the week. That’s four hundred pounds, cash on delivery.

business-foundations-5/beat-02.text: Of course, one moment. Ah, there’s forty pounds and a button.

business-foundations-5/beat-03.text: Your customers pay after they fly, and the gas is due before anybody does. You can’t pay a bill with profit on paper.

business-foundations-5/beat-05.text: Tell you what, keep two cylinders on trust till Friday. You can pay me then.

business-foundations-5/beat-06.text: Kind of him, and more than you deserve. From now on, take half the fare when people book, not after they land.

business-foundations-5/beat-07.text: Half up front. A brilliant idea, and I’ll tell everyone it was mine.

business-foundations-5/beat-08.text: And keep some cash in this tin, for the weeks when people pay late.

business-foundations-5/beat-10.text: Up we go, and the gas is paid for. Mostly.

business-foundations-6/beat-00.text: Welcome to Castle Fright! It’s opening night, and I’ve spent a fortune on cobwebs.

business-foundations-6/beat-01.text: Fifteen pounds a ticket, and every guest gets popcorn and a glow stick. Those cost us five pounds each.

business-foundations-6/beat-02.text: The castle, the actors and the lights cost a thousand pounds a night, however many people come.

business-foundations-6/beat-03.text: Costs that stay the same are fixed costs. Costs that grow with every guest are variable costs.

business-foundations-6/beat-05.text: So every ticket makes me ten pounds. I’m rich already!

business-foundations-6/beat-06.text: No. Each ticket leaves ten pounds after its own costs, and those tens pay off the thousand first.

business-foundations-6/beat-07.text: So the first guests pay for the castle, and only the later ones make any money?

business-foundations-6/beat-08.text: Right. The point where sales just cover every cost is the break-even point.

business-foundations-6/beat-10.text: Guest one hundred and one! Finally, a scream that pays.

economics-foundations-1/beat-00.text: One ten-pound note. And I want everything on this table.

economics-foundations-1/beat-01.text: Everyone does, mate. The pie is six pounds, and the book is eight.

economics-foundations-1/beat-02.text: You two are doing economics, you know. Economics is the study of how people choose, when they can’t have it all.

economics-foundations-1/beat-03.text: Your wants never run out, but your money, your time and the bread on that stall all do. That gap is called scarcity.

economics-foundations-1/beat-06.text: Every choice has an opportunity cost. Spend an hour at this market, and you can’t spend that hour anywhere else.

economics-foundations-1/beat-07.text: One loaf left, and two hungry customers. Right, time to think about my price.

economics-foundations-2/beat-00.text: Umbrellas, five pounds each, anyone? Well, the sunshine is lovely, at least.

economics-foundations-2/beat-01.text: Oh, it’s pouring! I’ll take one, and so will everybody behind me.

economics-foundations-2/beat-02.text: The umbrellas haven’t changed, but how many people want one has. Economists call that demand.

economics-foundations-2/beat-03.text: Demand is how much people want to buy, at each price. When the rain starts, it jumps.

economics-foundations-2/beat-05.text: Three left, and a queue round the corner. I hate to do it, but they’re twelve pounds now.

economics-foundations-2/beat-06.text: That’s the other half: supply, how much sellers have to offer. Few umbrellas and many buyers make a high price.

economics-foundations-2/beat-07.text: Oh, look, a van full of umbrellas has just pulled up! Isn’t that lucky for him?

economics-foundations-2/beat-09.text: Six pounds, then, and everybody stays dry. Fair enough, I say.

economics-foundations-3/beat-00.text: The concert or the football. Both on Saturday afternoon, naturally.

economics-foundations-3/beat-01.text: The football’s free this week, mate. You can’t beat free!

economics-foundations-3/beat-02.text: Free costs no money, but it still costs something. Whichever one you choose, you give up the other.

economics-foundations-3/beat-03.text: Economists call what you give up the opportunity cost. It’s the next best thing you could have done instead.

economics-foundations-3/beat-05.text: So the free match would cost me a concert. How generous of it.

economics-foundations-3/beat-06.text: Yes. Your time is scarce too, so even a free afternoon has a price: everything else you could do with it.

economics-foundations-3/beat-07.text: The concert tickets are twenty pounds, if that helps at all.

economics-foundations-3/beat-08.text: Then weigh each choice against what it makes you give up. Pick the one that’s worth more to you than its cost.

economics-foundations-3/beat-10.text: One concert ticket, please. I’ll try not to enjoy it too much.

economics-foundations-4/beat-00.text: I’m growing tomatoes and keeping a hen this year. The hen is eating the tomatoes.

economics-foundations-4/beat-01.text: I’ve more eggs than I can eat. Swap you a box for a few tomatoes?

economics-foundations-4/beat-02.text: That swap is the whole idea of trade. Each of you makes what you’re good at, then you exchange.

economics-foundations-4/beat-03.text: Doing one job well is called specialising. She grows tomatoes, he keeps hens, and nobody does both badly.

economics-foundations-4/beat-05.text: So I give him tomatoes, and he gives me eggs. And I don’t have to talk to the hen.

economics-foundations-4/beat-06.text: You both end up with more than you’d make doing everything yourselves. Trade isn’t one side winning.

economics-foundations-4/beat-07.text: Fresh tomatoes for my sandwiches. I couldn’t grow one of these if I tried.

economics-foundations-4/beat-09.text: Then my hen should live with his hens. She’ll be much happier there, I think.

economics-foundations-5/beat-00.text: As mayor, I’ve solved the rat problem. One silver coin for every rat tail brought to me.

economics-foundations-5/beat-01.text: Fifty tails today! I’m the best rat catcher in town, and I’ve hardly left my cellar.

economics-foundations-5/beat-02.text: You’ve solved nothing. There are more rats in this town than last month, and I think I know why.

economics-foundations-5/beat-04.text: My rat farm! Two rats make twenty, and twenty make a basket of easy money.

economics-foundations-5/beat-05.text: A reward that changes what people do is called an incentive. People chase the reward, not what you meant by it.

economics-foundations-5/beat-06.text: You put a price on tails, so the town started making them. It’s supply rising with the price, like any market.

economics-foundations-5/beat-07.text: So it’s the rats’ fault, for having so many babies. Clever little things.

economics-foundations-5/beat-08.text: No. Pay for what you want, not for something that’s easy to make more of.

economics-foundations-5/beat-10.text: No rats, no coins? Then I’ll go back to growing cabbages.

economics-foundations-6/beat-00.text: Treasure! I’ve shared it with every pirate on the island. I’m the most generous captain alive.

economics-foundations-6/beat-01.text: Everyone’s waving gold at my coconuts, and I’ve only got twelve. So I’ve doubled my price.

economics-foundations-6/beat-02.text: The coconuts didn’t get any better. There’s just more gold chasing the same twelve coconuts.

economics-foundations-6/beat-04.text: When prices rise across the board like that, it’s called inflation. Your gold buys less than it did.

economics-foundations-6/beat-05.text: So my treasure made everyone poorer? Impossible. I’m a hero.

economics-foundations-6/beat-06.text: Not poorer in gold. Poorer in what gold can buy, and money is only worth the things you can get with it.

economics-foundations-6/beat-07.text: So how do I get my old prices back? I liked being a one-coin coconut lady.

economics-foundations-6/beat-09.text: Then I’m burying the rest of it again, for the good of the economy.

history-foundations-1/beat-00.text: My window! It was whole when I locked up, so it must have been the wind.

history-foundations-1/beat-01.text: Oh, brilliant, you found my ball! It’s right there, in your window.

history-foundations-1/beat-02.text: Nobody here saw it break, and the past is gone. All it leaves behind is evidence, and that’s where history starts.

history-foundations-1/beat-03.text: It can’t have been me, I only kicked it once. Quite hard, towards the shop.

history-foundations-1/beat-05.text: Then ask who’s telling each story. Every source has a point of view, so a historian asks who’s speaking, and why.

history-foundations-1/beat-06.text: No harm meant, I’m sure. Still, somebody ought to pay for the glass, and I hate to ask.

history-foundations-1/beat-07.text: Now the question isn’t what happened, but who decides what happens next. That’s politics.

history-foundations-1/beat-09.text: We could make a rule: whoever kicks the ball pays for the window! Oh, no.

history-foundations-2/beat-00.text: My great-grandad captured a whole castle by himself! It says so, right here in this book.

history-foundations-2/beat-01.text: How thrilling. Then why does his own letter say he spent that week peeling potatoes?

history-foundations-2/beat-02.text: Your letter and her book disagree, then. A historian’s first question is when each one was made, and by whom.

history-foundations-2/beat-03.text: A source made at the time, by someone who was there, is a primary source. One written later, from other sources, is a secondary source.

history-foundations-2/beat-05.text: But the book is printed, with pictures and everything. Printed things are true, aren’t they?

history-foundations-2/beat-06.text: Printed isn’t the same as checked. When two sources disagree, a historian looks for a third from the time, to see which story it backs.

history-foundations-2/beat-08.text: The local paper from that very week is in the box too. No castles, I’m afraid, but a great many potatoes.

history-foundations-2/beat-09.text: So he fed the whole regiment! That makes me even prouder.

history-foundations-3/beat-00.text: I only drove over it, honest. Same as every market day for twenty years!

history-foundations-3/beat-01.text: And the bridge picked today to give up. How thoughtful of it.

history-foundations-3/beat-02.text: Historians ask why things happened, and the answer is nearly always more than one cause.

history-foundations-3/beat-03.text: This plank has been rotting for years. That’s a long-term cause, building up before anyone noticed.

history-foundations-3/beat-05.text: So it wasn’t my cart at all, then? Oh, that’s a relief.

history-foundations-3/beat-06.text: Your cart was the trigger: the event on the day that set it off. Without the rot, the bridge would have held.

history-foundations-3/beat-07.text: And without the cart, it would have rotted for another year. Lovely.

history-foundations-3/beat-08.text: That’s why historians weigh their causes. They ask which one mattered most, and which one only set things off.

history-foundations-3/beat-10.text: Then I’ll mend the plank myself, and go round by the ford until it’s done.

history-foundations-4/beat-00.text: I found a photo of this square from a hundred years ago. Everything’s different!

history-foundations-4/beat-01.text: Naturally. I’d have improved it too, if they’d asked me.

history-foundations-4/beat-02.text: Not everything. The clock tower is in the photo, and it’s still standing.

history-foundations-4/beat-03.text: What alters over time is called change, and what stays the same is called continuity. Historians look for both.

history-foundations-4/beat-05.text: The horse trough is full of flowers now. Did the horses just leave?

history-foundations-4/beat-06.text: Cars replaced the horses, bit by bit, over about thirty years. Some changes take a lifetime.

history-foundations-4/beat-07.text: And the bakery became a phone shop in one afternoon. That one, I fully approve of.

history-foundations-4/beat-08.text: Of course you do. Some change is quick, some is slow, and some things barely change at all.

history-foundations-5/beat-00.text: Ugh. What time is it? I don’t even remember falling asleep.

history-foundations-5/beat-01.text: Wait. My lamp, my poster, my hands. So why can I hear a crowd outside?

history-foundations-5/beat-02.text: Hello? Is somebody out there? I’m coming out, alright?

history-foundations-5/beat-03.text: At last! Citizens of Athens, the defendant has finally woken up.

history-foundations-5/beat-04.text: Defendant? Mate, I’ve just got out of bed. What am I supposed to have done?

history-foundations-5/beat-05.text: You wandered into Athens uninvited, and you’re suspiciously nice to everyone. I’m prosecuting you myself.

history-foundations-5/beat-06.text: Here, any citizen can bring a case. And look who’s judging you: five hundred ordinary men, picked by lottery this morning.

history-foundations-5/beat-07.text: No judge at all? Just a crowd of strangers who drew straws?

history-foundations-5/beat-08.text: Yes. Since you’re so curious, tell the court. Why a lottery?

history-foundations-5/beat-10.text: If nobody knows who’s judging until this morning, nobody can bribe them. That’s clever.

history-foundations-5/beat-11.text: So the cleverest people end up on the jury? That seems sensible to me.

history-foundations-5/beat-12.text: Correct. How disappointing. I was looking forward to watching you fail.

history-foundations-5/beat-13.text: A lottery picks the clever ones? You absolute turnip, it’s so nobody can bribe them!

history-foundations-5/beat-14.text: Now defend yourself. No lawyer will save you here: you speak for yourself, and this water clock times you.

history-foundations-5/beat-15.text: A clock made of water? And does it time you as well?

history-foundations-5/beat-16.text: Sadly, yes. Now prove you were listening, if you can.

history-foundations-5/beat-18.text: Same water for both of us, so neither of us gets longer to talk. That’s fair.

history-foundations-5/beat-19.text: So the jury can get home for dinner? Fair enough, they look hungry.

history-foundations-5/beat-20.text: Correct again. Do you practise being this annoying?

history-foundations-5/beat-21.text: Dinner? It’s so the time is fair, you hopeless lump. Equal water, equal time.

history-foundations-5/beat-22.text: Look, I don’t know how I got here. But I’ve been polite all morning, and he’s been rude, so you decide.

history-foundations-5/beat-23.text: Jurors, your discs: hollow means guilty, solid means innocent. Into the bronze urn with them.

history-foundations-5/beat-24.text: Three hundred solid discs: not guilty. I hate this city.

history-foundations-5/beat-25.text: Two hundred and fifty each way: a tie, and a tie means you go free. Ridiculous rule.

history-foundations-5/beat-26.text: Three hundred hollow discs. Guilty! Oh, this is the best day of my life.

history-foundations-5/beat-27.text: Right. I’m going back to bed. Wake me up when it’s a normal day.

history-foundations-6/beat-00.text: Look at him! Ramesses, alone in his chariot, beating the whole Hittite army.

history-foundations-6/beat-01.text: Funny thing. This tablet from the Hittite capital says the Hittites won.

history-foundations-6/beat-02.text: Then the tablet’s wrong. It’s made of mud.

history-foundations-6/beat-03.text: Every source was made by someone, for a reason. Ramesses had this carved on his own temple, for everyone to see.

history-foundations-6/beat-05.text: And the Hittite king wanted to look good too. So you check one side’s story against the other’s.

history-foundations-6/beat-06.text: So both kings claim the win? My brothers do that after a game of cards.

history-foundations-6/beat-07.text: Where the two sides agree, you can trust it more. The battle had no clear winner, and years later the kings signed a peace treaty.

history-foundations-6/beat-08.text: So he drew himself ten times bigger than everyone. I think that’s lovely.

history-foundations-6/beat-10.text: Mud tablets, one. Giant carvings, nil.

personal-growth-foundations-1/beat-00.text: New me! I’m growing the tallest sunflower on the street, starting today.

personal-growth-foundations-1/beat-01.text: How lovely. And how often will you water it?

personal-growth-foundations-1/beat-02.text: No need to water it often. Here’s a whole month of water, all in one go!

personal-growth-foundations-1/beat-03.text: No, no, it’s fine, mine only gets a cupful each morning. I’m sure yours knows best.

personal-growth-foundations-1/beat-04.text: You’ve each got your own idea of how change works. Personal growth is the study of how people change, on purpose.

personal-growth-foundations-1/beat-06.text: A little every day beats a lot all at once. The size of the step hardly matters, but coming back to it does.

personal-growth-foundations-1/beat-07.text: But I always forget! The watering can lives in the shed, behind the bikes.

personal-growth-foundations-1/beat-08.text: Then don’t try harder, make it easier. Put the can where you can’t miss it.

personal-growth-foundations-1/beat-10.text: A cupful a day. It’s almost as if the boring way works.

personal-growth-foundations-2/beat-00.text: Three o’clock already! Time for a cup of tea, and just the one biscuit.

personal-growth-foundations-2/beat-01.text: Just the one, at three, every day this week. Not that I’ve been counting.

personal-growth-foundations-2/beat-02.text: The man with the biscuit isn’t even hungry. He’s caught in a habit, and every habit runs on a loop.

personal-growth-foundations-2/beat-03.text: A cue starts it, and the routine is what you do. The reward at the end makes you want to do it again.

personal-growth-foundations-2/beat-05.text: I suppose it’s the break I’m after. Ten quiet minutes, and a sit down.

personal-growth-foundations-2/beat-06.text: Then keep the cue, and keep the reward. Change only the routine in the middle.

personal-growth-foundations-2/beat-07.text: Or he could stop. Willpower, I believe it’s called.

personal-growth-foundations-2/beat-08.text: Fighting a cue every single day is hard work. A swap is easier, because the habit still gets what it came for.

personal-growth-foundations-2/beat-10.text: An apple and a cup of tea, then. Do you know, it’s the sitting down I like best.

personal-growth-foundations-3/beat-00.text: This year, I’m getting fit! I’ll start properly once the weather’s warmer.

personal-growth-foundations-3/beat-01.text: Same goal as last year, I believe. And the year before that.

personal-growth-foundations-3/beat-02.text: Getting fit is a wish, not a goal. A goal is specific, so you can tell when you’ve done it.

personal-growth-foundations-3/beat-03.text: Run once round this track without stopping. That one you can check, today, with a stopwatch.

personal-growth-foundations-3/beat-05.text: Only one lap? That sounds almost too easy, to be honest.

personal-growth-foundations-3/beat-06.text: Good. Make the first step small enough to start today, then make it a little bigger each week.

personal-growth-foundations-3/beat-07.text: And when is this lap happening, then? I only ask.

personal-growth-foundations-3/beat-08.text: That’s the last part. Write down when and where, and put it somewhere you’ll see it every day.

personal-growth-foundations-3/beat-10.text: Tuesday, half past seven, one lap. Oh, I’ll even bring the proper trainers!

personal-growth-foundations-4/beat-00.text: Behold. My very first pot, and already a masterpiece.

personal-growth-foundations-4/beat-01.text: My pot’s fallen over. That wheel must be broken.

personal-growth-foundations-4/beat-02.text: Your clay’s too wet, mate. Feel how soft the walls are.

personal-growth-foundations-4/beat-03.text: Blaming the wheel teaches you nothing. A mistake is information, if you look at what went wrong.

personal-growth-foundations-4/beat-05.text: Too much water. I’d have spotted that myself, eventually.

personal-growth-foundations-4/beat-06.text: Then change one thing and try again. Less water, same wheel, and please, less talking.

personal-growth-foundations-4/beat-07.text: My pot is standing. You may all applaud now.

personal-growth-foundations-4/beat-08.text: Every pot on that shelf fell over a few times first. Mine certainly did.

personal-growth-foundations-4/beat-09.text: That’s how skill grows. Each mistake you learn from makes the next try a little better.

personal-growth-foundations-5/beat-00.text: Ten thousand times across this rope, and I’ve never wobbled once.

personal-growth-foundations-5/beat-01.text: That rope’s lying on the floor. You could cross it asleep, and you haven’t learned a thing in years.

personal-growth-foundations-5/beat-02.text: I’m skipping the boring bit. I’ll practise up on the high wire from day one!

personal-growth-foundations-5/beat-03.text: Down. Up there you’d be too scared to learn a thing, and you’d just cling on.

personal-growth-foundations-5/beat-04.text: You get better at the edge of what you can do. Hard enough that you wobble, safe enough that you can think.

personal-growth-foundations-5/beat-06.text: Whoa! I fell off four times, but I think I keep leaning to the left.

personal-growth-foundations-5/beat-07.text: Good, that’s the one to fix. Practise just the lean, and get told the moment it goes wrong.

personal-growth-foundations-5/beat-08.text: I’ll come up there too. If I can still wobble, I can still get better.

personal-growth-foundations-5/beat-10.text: Every time I lean, he blows the whistle. I hate the noise, and I’ve stopped leaning.

personal-growth-foundations-6/beat-00.text: I learned the whole Morse alphabet last night, in one go. Ask me anything!

personal-growth-foundations-6/beat-01.text: I’ve been doing ten minutes a day, all week. I’m still slow, mind.

personal-growth-foundations-6/beat-03.text: There’s a ship signalling out there. Read it to me, both of you, and be quick.

personal-growth-foundations-6/beat-04.text: Dot, dash, dot? I’ve forgotten nearly all of it!

personal-growth-foundations-6/beat-05.text: Three short, three long, three short. That’s S O S, they need help!

personal-growth-foundations-6/beat-06.text: Cramming fills your head for a night, then most of it drains away. Practice spread out over days is what stays.

personal-growth-foundations-6/beat-07.text: And each time you nearly forget and then remember, the memory gets stronger. So let the gaps grow.

personal-growth-foundations-6/beat-09.text: Fine, ten minutes a day. Starting tomorrow, I promise.

philosophy-foundations-1/beat-00.text: One squeaky wheel. That’s all I asked you to fix.

philosophy-foundations-1/beat-01.text: Fixed it, and the frame was cracked, so I changed that and the saddle too. No charge, mate.

philosophy-foundations-1/beat-02.text: How generous. So is this still my bicycle, or a stranger’s?

philosophy-foundations-1/beat-03.text: Now that’s a philosophy question. You two agree on every fact, and you still can’t agree on the answer.

philosophy-foundations-1/beat-04.text: Philosophy asks what we mean and what’s true, when looking harder won’t settle it.

philosophy-foundations-1/beat-06.text: I’d call the bicycle yours. Same owner, same stand, and it never left my sight.

philosophy-foundations-1/beat-07.text: And I’d say mine is in that crate, in pieces. But do go on.

philosophy-foundations-1/beat-08.text: Nobody shouted, and nobody took a vote. Each of them gave a reason, and a reason can be tested.

philosophy-foundations-1/beat-10.text: You already live by answers like these: what’s fair, what’s real and what you owe. Philosophy is how you check them.

philosophy-foundations-2/beat-00.text: One slice of carrot cake, please! Carrots are good for you, so carrot cake counts as healthy.

philosophy-foundations-2/beat-01.text: And butter, and sugar, and a thick layer of icing. Do enjoy your vegetables.

philosophy-foundations-2/beat-02.text: You’ve just made an argument, believe it or not. An argument is a set of reasons that support a conclusion.

philosophy-foundations-2/beat-03.text: The customer’s argument goes up on the board. Carrots are healthy, and this cake has carrots, so this cake is healthy.

philosophy-foundations-2/beat-05.text: A good argument needs two things. True reasons, and a conclusion that follows from them.

philosophy-foundations-2/beat-06.text: Well, she would say that. She has cake for breakfast.

philosophy-foundations-2/beat-07.text: That’s an attack on the person, not on the reasons. What she eats for breakfast doesn’t change a word on that board.

philosophy-foundations-2/beat-09.text: Oh! So my reasons were fine, and my conclusion wasn’t. I’m still finishing the cake.

philosophy-foundations-3/beat-00.text: Look what fell out of my library book! Twenty pounds, and no name on it anywhere.

philosophy-foundations-3/beat-01.text: Oh, the poor soul who lost that. I’ll pin a notice up, just in case.

philosophy-foundations-3/beat-02.text: Keep it, or hand it in? Philosophers have two main ways of deciding what’s right.

philosophy-foundations-3/beat-03.text: The first looks at consequences. You ask who your choice will help, and who it will harm.

philosophy-foundations-3/beat-05.text: But if nobody comes back for it, then everybody’s happy. Especially me!

philosophy-foundations-3/beat-06.text: The second way looks at rules. Some things are wrong whatever happens next, and taking what isn’t yours is one of them.

philosophy-foundations-3/beat-07.text: The rule’s on the wall, love. Anything found comes straight to the front desk.

philosophy-foundations-3/beat-08.text: Here, both ways agree. Each one asks you for a reason, and a good reason still holds when you say it out loud.

philosophy-foundations-3/beat-10.text: Fine, the note goes in the box. Goodbye, twenty pounds, you were lovely!

philosophy-foundations-4/beat-00.text: Quarter past nine, and my train is at half past. I always know these things.

philosophy-foundations-4/beat-01.text: That clock stopped at quarter past nine last night. Its hands haven’t moved since.

philosophy-foundations-4/beat-02.text: And yet it’s quarter past nine, so I was right. Again.

philosophy-foundations-4/beat-03.text: Being right isn’t the same as knowing. To know something, your belief must be true, and you need a good reason for it.

philosophy-foundations-4/beat-05.text: A lucky guess can be true. Luck isn’t a reason, though, so a lucky guess isn’t knowledge.

philosophy-foundations-4/beat-06.text: So I was right, and it doesn’t count. What a tragedy.

philosophy-foundations-4/beat-07.text: It counts once you check. Go and read the board, please, while I’m still young.

philosophy-foundations-4/beat-08.text: Half past nine, on time. Now I know it, and I’d like that written down somewhere.

philosophy-foundations-5/beat-00.text: The pod’s warmed up! It scans every atom of you, beams the plan to the Moon, and builds you there.

philosophy-foundations-5/beat-01.text: The first man ever to teleport. They’ll put my face on a stamp.

philosophy-foundations-5/beat-02.text: Oh, and the pod breaks the old you down for parts. We can’t have two of you walking around.

philosophy-foundations-5/beat-03.text: Now he hesitates. Whether the man on the Moon is you depends on what makes you you.

philosophy-foundations-5/beat-04.text: If you’re your body, you end here and a copy wakes up. If you’re your memories, you travel to the Moon.

philosophy-foundations-5/beat-06.text: Fine. My memories are magnificent anyway. Beam them up.

philosophy-foundations-5/beat-07.text: Oops, the recycler jammed. Now there’s one of him in here and one on the Moon!

philosophy-foundations-5/beat-08.text: I’m the real one. He’s a very handsome copy, but a copy.

philosophy-foundations-5/beat-09.text: And he’d say the same, with the same memories. One person can’t be two people, so memories alone can’t settle who’s you.

philosophy-foundations-6/beat-00.text: Step up! The oracle prints your choice before you’ve even made it.

philosophy-foundations-6/beat-01.text: Nobody predicts me, I’m a mystery even to myself. Fudge!

philosophy-foundations-6/beat-02.text: The card says fudge! It always knows.

philosophy-foundations-6/beat-03.text: Of course it does. You love fudge, you skipped lunch, and you hate being told what to do.

philosophy-foundations-6/beat-04.text: If every choice is caused by what came before it, could you ever have picked differently? That’s the puzzle of free will.

philosophy-foundations-6/beat-06.text: Then I’ll take the mint instead, just to spite it.

philosophy-foundations-6/beat-07.text: Oh, there’s a second card! It says, he’ll take the mint, just to spite me.

philosophy-foundations-6/beat-08.text: Here’s one answer. You’re free when you act on your own wants and nobody forces you, even if those wants have causes.

philosophy-foundations-6/beat-10.text: Then I’m free too. I’m freely choosing to eat all the toffee.

psychology-foundations-1/beat-00.text: I can always tell cheap coffee from the good stuff. Always.

psychology-foundations-1/beat-01.text: Perfect, two cups! This one’s from the bargain tin, and this one’s the gold label.

psychology-foundations-1/beat-02.text: The gold one, of course, so smooth. The other tastes like a wet sock.

psychology-foundations-1/beat-03.text: Oh, that’s funny, I only made one pot. They’re both the same coffee.

psychology-foundations-1/beat-04.text: It’s the same coffee, and it tasted different to him. The change happened in his head, and that’s where psychology looks.

psychology-foundations-1/beat-06.text: Psychology is the study of how people think, feel and act. Its first lesson is that we’re poor witnesses of our own minds.

psychology-foundations-1/beat-07.text: I’d have noticed, of course. If anyone had warned me it was a test.

psychology-foundations-1/beat-08.text: The taster is still sure, so a psychologist doesn’t ask him. You swap the labels, pour again and count what he does.

psychology-foundations-1/beat-10.text: The taster picked the gold one again, and that’s the bargain tin! Should I tell him?

psychology-foundations-2/beat-00.text: Oh, hello! I think our trolleys just met.

psychology-foundations-2/beat-01.text: Sorry, that was my fault. I was barely moving, but there goes your jam.

psychology-foundations-2/beat-02.text: This gentleman came flying round the corner, I promise you. I heard the glass break before I even saw him.

psychology-foundations-2/beat-03.text: You both saw the same bump, and you remember it differently. Neither of you is lying.

psychology-foundations-2/beat-04.text: A memory isn’t a recording. Each time you remember something, your brain builds it again, and fills the gaps with whatever seems to fit.

psychology-foundations-2/beat-06.text: The words of a question can change the memory itself. So a careful interviewer asks what happened, and lets the person tell it.

psychology-foundations-2/beat-07.text: Well, I’m certain I was barely moving. Though I suppose she’s just as certain.

psychology-foundations-2/beat-08.text: Feeling sure isn’t the same as being right. A story can feel more certain each time it’s told, even as the details drift.

psychology-foundations-2/beat-10.text: Oh, look, he was barely moving. So who broke my jam?

psychology-foundations-3/beat-00.text: Would you look at that. A royal cup, fourteen hundred years old, and every chip so delicate.

psychology-foundations-3/beat-01.text: Remarkable. That’s my tea mug, left on the plinth ten minutes ago.

psychology-foundations-3/beat-02.text: Your eyes take in the shapes, but your brain decides what the shapes mean. What you expect changes what you see.

psychology-foundations-3/beat-03.text: A label, a price or a hint sets that expectation before you even look. This label said royal.

psychology-foundations-3/beat-05.text: Well, now it just looks like a mug with a chip in it. Funny, that.

psychology-foundations-3/beat-06.text: To see what’s there, look again without the hint. Ask what you’d see if nobody had told you anything.

psychology-foundations-3/beat-07.text: Or read the sticker underneath. It says dishwasher safe.

psychology-foundations-3/beat-08.text: That’s the check. Trust the evidence from the thing itself, not what you were told about it.

psychology-foundations-3/beat-10.text: A dishwasher-safe treasure, then. I’ll still give it a nice look on my way out.

psychology-foundations-4/beat-00.text: The bus stop is very quiet this morning. Everyone must be on holiday.

psychology-foundations-4/beat-01.text: Oh good, someone’s waiting. This must be the right stop, then.

psychology-foundations-4/beat-02.text: Neither of you has read the notice on this post. The stop has been closed all week.

psychology-foundations-4/beat-03.text: Oh, I’m sorry. I only stopped here because I saw her waiting.

psychology-foundations-4/beat-04.text: When people are unsure what to do, they copy what others are doing. Psychologists call it social proof.

psychology-foundations-4/beat-06.text: Copying is often sensible. A queue outside a café usually means the coffee is good.

psychology-foundations-4/beat-07.text: So he copied me, and I felt sure because he came. That sounds like teamwork to me.

psychology-foundations-4/beat-08.text: No. When everybody copies everybody, nobody checks. A crowd can be wrong all together.

psychology-foundations-4/beat-10.text: The new stop is round the corner. Come on, I’ll walk you both there.

psychology-foundations-5/beat-00.text: At midnight a saucer lands on this hill and takes us away. They told me personally.

psychology-foundations-5/beat-01.text: I sold my car to be here, and I baked them a lemon cake. I hope they like lemon.

psychology-foundations-5/beat-02.text: I study how people think. I’m here to see what they do when midnight comes and nothing lands.

psychology-foundations-5/beat-04.text: Our faith was so strong, they called the whole thing off. I’ve saved the world, and you’re welcome.

psychology-foundations-5/beat-05.text: Oh, thank goodness. Then I didn’t sell my car for nothing.

psychology-foundations-5/beat-06.text: Two thoughts are clashing in his head: the saucer was coming, and nothing came. That clash hurts, and it’s called cognitive dissonance.

psychology-foundations-5/beat-07.text: The easy way out isn’t to drop the belief. It’s to change the story, so the belief survives.

psychology-foundations-5/beat-08.text: And the more a belief has cost you, the harder you’ll cling to it. He sold his car for this one.

psychology-foundations-5/beat-10.text: Right, new date, next Tuesday. I’ll need more posters, and a lot more followers.

psychology-foundations-6/beat-00.text: So close! Again, I’ll win the purple bear this time.

psychology-foundations-6/beat-01.text: My finest machine. It lets you win just often enough to keep the coins coming.

psychology-foundations-6/beat-02.text: That’s no accident. When a reward comes matters as much as the reward itself.

psychology-foundations-6/beat-04.text: A reward makes you more likely to do a thing again, and psychologists call that reinforcement. It works best when you can’t tell when it’s coming.

psychology-foundations-6/beat-05.text: I won! Now I just need the green one.

psychology-foundations-6/beat-06.text: Of course you do, nobody walks out after a win. I designed it that way, beautifully.

psychology-foundations-6/beat-07.text: Your phone does the same thing. Pull the screen down, and sometimes there’s something new.

psychology-foundations-6/beat-09.text: So my phone’s a claw machine I carry around. Right, I’m going home, straight after one more go.

science-foundations-1/beat-00.text: The heavy ball lands first, of course. Everybody knows that.

science-foundations-1/beat-01.text: Could be, mate. I’m up the ladder anyway, so I’ll drop them both and we’ll see.

science-foundations-1/beat-02.text: Before he lets go, make your own guess. Science starts with a guess you’re willing to test.

science-foundations-1/beat-04.text: There you go, both at once. Sorry, mate.

science-foundations-1/beat-05.text: No, no, it’s fine. I’m sure heavy things fell faster when I was young.

science-foundations-1/beat-06.text: Being certain didn’t save him, and one drop settled it. In science, the test beats the argument.

science-foundations-1/beat-07.text: And a real test is one your guess could fail. That risk is what makes the answer worth trusting.

science-foundations-1/beat-09.text: Ideas that pass their tests get built on. That’s technology: tested knowledge put to work, like the ladder he’s standing on.

science-foundations-2/beat-00.text: Mine has the pointy nose, so it’ll fly the furthest. Watch this!

science-foundations-2/beat-01.text: Off you go, then. Goodness, it went miles, and mine barely made it past my feet!

science-foundations-2/beat-02.text: So that’s settled, then. Pointy noses fly further!

science-foundations-2/beat-03.text: Not yet, I’m afraid. She threw from the top of the steps, and he threw from the grass.

science-foundations-2/beat-04.text: A fair test changes one thing, and keeps everything else the same. Then you know what made the difference.

science-foundations-2/beat-06.text: Shall we both throw from this line, then? Same paper, same arm, nice and gentle.

science-foundations-2/beat-07.text: Mine won again! Only by a little, but it still won.

science-foundations-2/beat-08.text: One throw can be luck, a gust or a wobble. Repeat it many times, and the luck starts to cancel out.

science-foundations-2/beat-10.text: Ten throws each, and we’ll chalk up every one. Lovely day for it!

science-foundations-3/beat-00.text: Look at the chart! When ice cream sales go up, so does sunburn, so ice cream must burn you!

science-foundations-3/beat-01.text: Yes, I’ve always found my cornet terribly hot.

science-foundations-3/beat-02.text: The two lines do rise together. That’s called a correlation, and it doesn’t mean one causes the other.

science-foundations-3/beat-03.text: Often a hidden cause pushes both of them up. Here, it’s the thing everybody came to the seaside for.

science-foundations-3/beat-05.text: Oh, sunny days! More people out buying ice cream, and more people out in the sun.

science-foundations-3/beat-06.text: To show that one thing causes another, change only that thing. Then watch whether the other one follows.

science-foundations-3/beat-07.text: So a whole afternoon of ice cream in the shade. I’ll volunteer.

science-foundations-3/beat-08.text: Eat ice cream in the shade, and the sunburn won’t come. Sit out in the sun without any, and it will.

science-foundations-3/beat-10.text: Sun cream, then, and an ice cream anyway. Science is delicious!

science-foundations-4/beat-00.text: One swing took three seconds. That’s the experiment done, then!

science-foundations-4/beat-01.text: One measurement is a start, not an answer. Time it again, and again.

science-foundations-4/beat-02.text: Two point eight, and now three point one. The swing keeps changing its mind!

science-foundations-4/beat-03.text: The swing is steady. Every measurement has a small error, and yours comes from your thumb on the button.

science-foundations-4/beat-05.text: So you measure several times and take the average. The small errors cancel each other out.

science-foundations-4/beat-06.text: I got two seconds once, while a dog ran past. Shall I just rub that one out?

science-foundations-4/beat-07.text: Don’t hide it. A result far from the others means something went wrong, so find out what and measure again.

science-foundations-4/beat-09.text: The average of my three good ones is about three seconds. So I was right all along!

science-foundations-5/beat-00.text: Tonight we finally get proof of the monster. Row us out to the middle!

science-foundations-5/beat-01.text: The sonar’s clear, and the camera’s caught nothing. Sorry, I’ve looked everywhere.

science-foundations-5/beat-02.text: That’s because she hides whenever she’s watched. And she doesn’t show up on sonar.

science-foundations-5/beat-03.text: So if she’s seen, she’s real, and if she isn’t seen, she’s still real. Nothing could ever count against her.

science-foundations-5/beat-04.text: A claim that can’t be wrong tells you nothing. Science needs claims that could fail a test, and that’s called falsifiability.

science-foundations-5/beat-06.text: Fine. She’s ten metres long, and she lives right here in this loch.

science-foundations-5/beat-07.text: Good. Now look hardest for the result that would prove you wrong, not the one that saves you.

science-foundations-5/beat-08.text: I’ll sweep the loch end to end, every night for a month. I’ve brought a flask.

science-foundations-5/beat-10.text: A whole month of nothing. Maybe she’s moved to the next loch over.

science-foundations-6/beat-00.text: My gums are sore and my old cuts have opened up again. Half the crew’s the same.

science-foundations-6/beat-01.text: My own seawater tonic will fix them. I’ve never tested it, because I’ve never needed to.

science-foundations-6/beat-02.text: Then we’ll test it. Twelve sick men, all on the same food, in pairs, and each pair gets a different remedy.

science-foundations-6/beat-03.text: Two get your seawater, two get vinegar, two get oranges and lemons, and so on.

science-foundations-6/beat-05.text: Six days of oranges and lemons, and I’m back on deck dancing!

science-foundations-6/beat-06.text: Lucky. My seawater men are just as sick, so they weren’t trying hard enough.

science-foundations-6/beat-07.text: Comparing groups treated differently is how you know it was the lemons, not luck or the weather.

science-foundations-6/beat-08.text: But a man who’s sure his medicine works can feel better from hope alone. That could fool us too.

science-foundations-6/beat-10.text: Then I’ll write miracle cure on mine. Problem solved.
